title: The recall notice at 2:10
note: Fictional unit and supplier. The recall notice’s own instructions, your unit’s procedure and the physician’s orders come first.
intro: You are the head nurse. At 14:10 on Friday, the supplier emails a recall notice for dialyzer lot 24K118, a size many of your patients use: a manufacturing defect may cause fibers to break and leak blood. The notice says to stop using the lot, quarantine remaining stock, and return it. Twelve second-shift patients are on the machines. The third shift starts at 16:00.

choices.text: Search the lot log, pull every box of 24K118, and tell the physician on duty.
choices.feedback: Recording lot numbers for each patient and session is what turns a recall into a fifteen-minute task. The log tells you who is exposed now and who was before; quarantining the stock stops the next exposure; the physician decides what happens to the patients.
choices.then: The lot was used in 11 sessions over three days, for 8 patients. Two of them are connected now, at stations 4 and 9. Every remaining box is moved to quarantine.

choices.text: Phone the supplier’s representative to ask how serious the defect is before alarming the staff or the physician on a busy Friday.
choices.feedback: The notice already tells you what to do. Asking the representative can come later; the log, the quarantine and the physician cannot wait.
choices.then: The representative does not answer. You search the log: 11 sessions, 8 patients, two connected now at stations 4 and 9. You quarantine the stock and call the physician.

choices.text: Post the notice at the nurses’ station.
choices.feedback: A posted notice does not find exposed patients or take stock off the shelf. Someone has to own the recall, and that is you.
choices.then: A nurse opens a new box of the lot for the third shift before you stop her. You search the log, quarantine the stock, and call the physician.

n2.scene: Both patients have about 90 minutes left. Neither machine has a blood-leak alarm, and both are comfortable.
n2.prompt: What do you do about them?

choices.text: Have both checked now and let the physician decide whether to change the dialyzer.
choices.feedback: Whether to stop, change the dialyzer, or finish the session is a medical decision. Your part is to make sure both patients and their circuits are looked at now, and that the nurses know what a blood-leak alarm would mean today.
choices.then: The physician orders a dialyzer change for both at the next safe point, using a different lot.

choices.text: Leave them to finish, since there has been no blood-leak alarm and the detector would catch a broken fiber.
choices.feedback: The detector is a safety net, not a plan. The physician has to know these two patients are on a recalled lot and decide.
choices.then: You tell the physician. He orders a dialyzer change for both, using a different lot.

choices.text: Tell both nurses to watch the dialysate line and the blood-leak alarm closely for the rest of the session, and report anything.
choices.feedback: Closer watching helps, but the decision about the dialyzers is the physician’s, and he needs to make it now.
choices.then: You call the physician, who orders a dialyzer change for both.

n3.scene: Six third-shift patients are prescribed this dialyzer size. After the quarantine, one box of another lot is left: four dialyzers. The next delivery is Monday.

choices.text: Ask the physician for an approved substitute, and borrow from a partner unit.
choices.feedback: Changing the dialyzer is a prescription change, so the physician writes it. A partner unit or the supplier’s emergency stock can close the gap. Patients who have just had a two-day weekend ahead of them should not lose a session.
choices.then: The physician approves a substitute size the unit has in stock for two patients; a partner unit sends a box of the original model by 15:45.

choices.text: Use the recalled lot for the last two patients after a careful visual check and a pressure test of each dialyzer, since the notice says only that fibers “may” break.
choices.feedback: A recalled lot is out of use. A defect that “may” occur is exactly what a visual check cannot exclude.
choices.then: The physician stops it. He approves a substitute size for two patients, and a partner unit sends a box by 15:45.

choices.text: Move two patients to Saturday morning.
choices.feedback: Postponing is a medical decision, and it lengthens the gap for patients who may already be at their limit. Look for a substitute or a loan first.
choices.then: The physician prefers a substitute. He approves a different size for two patients, and a partner unit sends a box.

n4.scene: Six more patients used the lot earlier in the week. Going through their session records, you see that one, Mr. Abad, had chills and a blood-leak alarm on Wednesday; the dialyzer was changed and the note says “resolved.”
n4.prompt: What do you do with this?

choices.text: Give the physician the full list, with Mr. Abad’s Wednesday event marked.
choices.feedback: The physician decides who needs a call, a check or tests. Mr. Abad’s event now looks like a possible product failure rather than a one-off, and it may need to be reported to the supplier and in your incident system.

choices.text: Phone all six patients yourself this afternoon.
choices.feedback: Checking on them may be right, but the physician decides what follow-up is needed and what to say. Give him the list first.
choices.then: You stop after the first call and give the physician the list, with Mr. Abad’s event marked.

choices.feedback: A recall reaches back to everyone exposed. Mr. Abad’s Wednesday alarm may be the defect itself.
choices.then: On reflection, you give the physician the list and Mr. Abad’s event.

choices.text: Return the stock as the notice says, record every step, and report Mr. Abad’s event.
choices.feedback: Return or hold the stock exactly as the notice instructs, record the count and who handled it, report the Wednesday event through your incident system and to the supplier, and bring the recall to the next quality meeting.

choices.text: Throw the quarantined boxes away so nobody can use them by mistake over the weekend while you are off.
choices.feedback: Quarantine already prevents use. Discarding stock loses the count and the evidence the supplier and regulators may need. Follow the notice.

choices.text: Return the stock to the supplier as the notice says, and file the notice with the unit’s supply records.
choices.feedback: Returning the stock is right, but without a record of who was exposed, a report of Mr. Abad’s event, and a review at the quality meeting, the recall is not closed.

end.title: The next Monday
end.text: The supplier confirms that Mr. Abad’s dialyzer was from the defective batch. The physician has already checked on all eight patients; none has a lasting problem. At the quality meeting, the unit agrees to keep the lot log exactly as it is: it turned the recall into an afternoon’s work.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Record lot numbers per patient and session. It is what lets a recall be traced in minutes.
  • Quarantine first, then follow the notice for return.
  • Patients on the lot are a medical decision: make sure the physician knows at once.
  • A recall reaches back to everyone exposed, and may explain an earlier event.
  • Close the loop: records, incident report, quality meeting.
